## Lab: Model Averaging using `mtcars` Data

In this lab, we will explore the concepts of model averaging. We'll use the `mtcars` dataset to predict miles per gallon (`mpg`), which is a regression task. We will build an "ensemble" of different models and show how a weighted average of their predictions can outperform any single model.

Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it. Packages load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds on first load.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)

data(mtcars)
head(mtcars)
```

---

### Individual Models

We will create our "ensemble" by training four different types of models to predict `mpg`. We'll use 10-fold cross-validation (CV) to get reliable performance estimates (RMSE) for each one.

```{webr}
library(caret)

set.seed(42)
train_control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

# Model 1: Simple Linear Regression (LM)
model_lm <- train(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars,
                  method = "lm", trControl = train_control)

# Model 2: LASSO Regression (a regularized model)
model_lasso <- train(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars,
                     method = "glmnet", trControl = train_control,
                     tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha = 1, lambda = seq(0.01, 1, length = 100)))

# Model 3: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) (a non-linear model)
model_knn <- train(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars,
                   method = "knn", trControl = train_control,
                   tuneLength = 5)

# Model 4: Decision Tree (rpart)
model_tree <- train(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars,
                    method = "rpart", trControl = train_control,
                    tuneLength = 5)

# Collect the results
results <- resamples(list(LM = model_lm, LASSO = model_lasso, KNN = model_knn, TREE = model_tree))

# What is the "best" model from our CV?
dotplot(results)
```

---

### Model Averaging

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggsci)

# Get predictions (Y-hat) from each model
predictions <- data.frame(
  truth = mtcars$mpg,
  lm = predict(model_lm, mtcars),
  lasso = predict(model_lasso, mtcars),
  knn = predict(model_knn, mtcars),
  tree = predict(model_tree, mtcars)
)
head(predictions)

# Average predictions -- option 1: unweighted average
predictions$unweighted_average <- apply(predictions[, -1], 1, mean)

# Average predictions -- option 2: weighted average, weighted by inverse RMSE
# (higher-error models get lower contribution)
weights <- 1 / (results$values |> select(contains("RMSE")) |> colMeans())
weights <- weights / sum(weights) # standardize so weights sum to 1

predictions$weighted_average <- as.matrix(predictions[, -c(1, 5)]) %*% (weights)

RMSE_vals <- results$values |> select(contains("RMSE")) |> colMeans()
RMSE_vals <- c(RMSE_vals, `Unweighted~RMSE` = RMSE(predictions$unweighted_average, predictions$truth))
RMSE_vals <- c(RMSE_vals, `Weighted~RMSE` = RMSE(predictions$weighted_average, predictions$truth))

RMSE_vals

as_tibble(predictions) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -truth) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = truth, y = value, color = name)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(name)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  scale_color_aaas()
```

**Interpretation:** The weighted average (weighted by each model's inverse cross-validated RMSE) typically beats every individual model, including the single best one from the CV comparison — this is the core intuition behind ensembling: uncorrelated errors partially cancel when averaged, so a blend of mediocre-but-different models can outperform any one strong model.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_weighting
# Try equal weights instead of inverse-RMSE weights -- does the ensemble still win?
custom_weights <- c(lm = ______, lasso = ______, knn = ______, tree = ______)   # try: 0.25 each (equal weighting)
custom_weights <- custom_weights / sum(custom_weights)

predictions$custom_average <- as.matrix(predictions[, c("lm", "lasso", "knn", "tree")]) %*% custom_weights
cat("Custom-weighted RMSE:", RMSE(predictions$custom_average, predictions$truth), "\n")
cat("Original weighted RMSE:", RMSE(predictions$weighted_average, predictions$truth), "\n")
```

**Live-coding demo:** fill in four equal weights (`0.25` each) and compare the resulting RMSE to the inverse-RMSE-weighted version above. Then try putting almost all the weight on just one model — at what point does "ensembling" stop helping and just become "using your best single model with extra steps"?
